title: Spend Controls and Business Cases for Technology
objectives: Navigate the post-RESET assurance landscape and Digital Assurance Playbook
Write compelling technology business cases using the Green Book five-case model
Understand when initiatives require Treasury Approval Process (TAP) panel review
Record initiatives on the Government Assurance Services pipeline effectively
Present architecture decisions in financial and strategic language for approval boards
whyThisMatters:
Architecture without funding is just a diagram. Every solution you design must eventually secure investment, navigate approval processes, and demonstrate value for money. In UK government, this means engaging with business case processes, understanding how assurance and approvals work, and being able to translate architectural choices into financial and strategic language.

The landscape changed fundamentally on 1 April 2026. The old central spend control process — where GDS approved digital and technology spending above defined thresholds — has been removed under the RESET framework. In its place, a more devolved model gives departments greater ownership of their approvals while introducing the Digital Assurance Playbook and the Government Assurance Services pipeline. The HM Treasury Green Book was also updated in 2026 following a significant review.

This lesson is not about turning architects into finance professionals. It is about ensuring you understand how the money works, because if you cannot articulate the financial case for your architecture decisions, those decisions will be made by people who can — and they may not make the choices you would.

content.heading: The Post-RESET Assurance and Approvals Landscape
content.body:
Before April 2026, any digital or technology spend above £100,000 for digital services or £1 million for technology required assurance through departmental boards and, above certain thresholds, central GDS approval. This process was detailed in the Digital and Technology Spend Controls Version 6.

The RESET framework changed this fundamentally. Digital and technology spend controls are removed. In their place, HM Treasury mandates that all organisations maintain and share a pipeline of upcoming spend and conduct appropriate functional assurance. Central approval from GDS is no longer needed for most spending — only for initiatives that exceed the organisation's Delegated Authority Limit (DAL) or that HM Treasury determines as being Novel, Contentious, or Repercussive (NCR).

Novel means initiatives the organisation has no experience of or that fall outside its normal course of business — for example, implementing AI in an organisation with no internal AI expertise. Contentious means initiatives that might cause debate or criticism by Parliament, the public, or media. Repercussive means initiatives likely to set a precedent or cause pressure across the wider public sector.

For initiatives below the DAL, organisations own and manage their own approvals journey. The Chief Digital and Information Officer is accountable to HM Treasury that the organisation maintains a pipeline viewable by assurers in GDS and HM Treasury.

The pipeline reporting threshold is £5 million whole life cost for digital and technology delivery, and £0 for cryptographic products. All initiatives above these thresholds must be recorded on the Government Assurance Services platform (which replaced the legacy Get Approval To Spend service).

For architects, this means: your architecture decisions still need to pass through approvals, but those approvals are now primarily internal to your department. The quality of your business case matters more than ever because there is no external check catching weak cases before money is committed.

content.heading: The Green Book Five-Case Model
content.body:
The HM Treasury Green Book is the government's guidance on how to appraise policies, programmes, and projects. It uses the five-case model as the recommended framework for developing business cases. Understanding this model is essential for any architect contributing to a technology business case.

The Strategic Case answers: why is this needed? It establishes the rationale for intervention, links to policy objectives and strategic priorities, describes the current situation and the problem to be solved, and demonstrates that doing nothing is not acceptable. The architect's contribution here is articulating the technology problem — legacy systems that cannot support new policy, technical debt that is blocking delivery, or architecture constraints that prevent service improvement.

The Economic Case answers: which option provides best value for money? This is where options appraisal lives. It presents a longlist of options, shortlists the most viable, and compares them on costs, benefits, risks, and value for money. The architect is central to this case — identifying realistic options, estimating their costs accurately, and honestly assessing their risks and benefits. The Economic Case requires quantified costs and benefits where possible, and should apply the Green Book's approach to optimism bias (adding a percentage uplift to cost estimates to account for the well-documented tendency to underestimate).

The Commercial Case answers: can this be procured? It describes how the preferred option will be delivered — whether through in-house capability, outsourcing, a framework agreement, or a combination. It considers market capacity, procurement route, and contract structure. The architect contributes by specifying what needs to be procured, what capabilities are needed from suppliers, and what constraints the architecture places on commercial options.

The Financial Case answers: is this affordable? It converts the Economic Case into actual cash flows, shows how the investment will be funded, and demonstrates affordability within departmental budgets. The architect needs to ensure their cost estimates are realistic, include whole-life costs (not just build costs), and account for ongoing operational expenditure.

The Management Case answers: can this be delivered? It describes the governance, delivery approach, risk management, and assurance arrangements. The architect contributes the technical delivery plan — phasing, dependencies, technical risks, and the approach to architecture governance during delivery.

content.heading: The Architect's Role in the Business Case
content.body:
Architects do not write business cases — that is typically the programme manager's or business analyst's job. But architects are essential contributors, and a business case without strong architectural input will fail in predictable ways.

The architect's primary contributions are: generating credible options for the Economic Case, producing realistic cost estimates for each option, identifying and quantifying technical risks, defining the delivery approach and phasing, and specifying the technical requirements that shape the Commercial Case.

Generating credible options requires genuine alternatives, not straw men. A business case with three options where two are obviously unsuitable is not a business case — it is advocacy disguised as analysis. Good options might include: a full rebuild, a phased modernisation, an extension of an existing platform, a commercial off-the-shelf solution, and a do-minimum option. Each should be genuinely viable and honestly assessed.

Realistic cost estimates are the architect's most important contribution and their most common failure. Architects consistently underestimate costs because they focus on build costs and forget: integration costs (always more than expected), data migration costs (always painful), testing costs (especially for security and performance testing), operational costs (hosting, monitoring, support contracts), training and change management costs, and the cost of decommissioning the thing being replaced.

Whole-life costing is essential. The Green Book requires costs over the entire lifecycle of the initiative. A cloud-native solution with low build cost but high annual operational cost may be more expensive over ten years than an on-premise solution with higher upfront cost but lower ongoing expense. The architecture directly determines this cost profile.

Optimism bias should be applied honestly. The Green Book provides guidance on appropriate optimism bias uplifts based on the type of project and its stage of development. For standard technology projects, an uplift of 10-25% to costs is typical at Outline Business Case stage. Architects should recommend appropriate uplift rather than presenting unbiased estimates and letting others decide — because the architect is best placed to judge how well-understood the technical scope is.

content.heading: Recording Initiatives on the Pipeline
content.body:
The Government Assurance Services pipeline is the mechanism through which organisations make their digital and technology spending visible. Recording your initiative on the pipeline is not a bureaucratic exercise — it is the trigger for accessing assurance support and the basis for demonstrating compliance with HM Treasury requirements.

What to record: programmes, projects, contracts, and early-stage ideas that may incur spend above the £5 million threshold. Individual Statements of Work do not need separate entries provided the overarching programme or contract is recorded. Ideas should be added when you know about them, even if they do not yet have a spend value.

When to record: at the earliest sensible time. Your organisation will have its own internal processes defining when initiatives are added. Some departments tie this to a Design Committee or equivalent early governance checkpoint. Others require recording when a Strategic Outline Case is being developed. The principle is early visibility — the earlier assurance colleagues can see what is coming, the earlier they can offer support.

What happens after recording: functional assurers in your organisation and potentially GDS may reach out to explore challenges and risks. For most initiatives below the DAL, this will be organisational assurance. For initiatives above the DAL or identified as high-risk, GDS central assurance will become involved.

The whole life cost calculation matters. The £5 million threshold is for cumulative cost across the entire lifecycle — initial capital plus ongoing operational expenses. For a service expected to run for five years, this includes all five years of cost. If a Business Case exists, use the figure from the Business Case. If not, use the spending envelope allocated through Business Planning or Spending Review.

As an architect, you are often the person best placed to calculate whole life cost for technology initiatives because you understand the cost drivers: hosting costs, licensing, support contracts, and the team size needed for ongoing development and operations.

content.heading: When Treasury Approval Is Needed
content.body:
Most digital and technology spending is now approved within departments. However, two categories still require HM Treasury approval through the Treasury Approval Process (TAP).

First, initiatives spending above the organisation's Delegated Authority Limit. DALs are set by HM Treasury for each organisation. They define the threshold of spend below which the organisation can independently approve. For most large departments, this is tens of millions of pounds. For smaller arm's length bodies, it may be significantly lower.

Second, initiatives deemed Novel, Contentious, or Repercussive by HM Treasury. This is a subjective judgement and can apply regardless of cost. A £2 million AI deployment that could attract public criticism might be deemed contentious. A £500,000 licensing deal that sets a precedent across government might be deemed repercussive.

The TAP process works as follows: if an initiative is flagged (by its spend exceeding the DAL, or by HM Treasury deeming it NCR), GDS central assurance engages to support the team through the Treasury approval step. This could be a desk-level review (normal for straightforward cases) or a TAP panel (for complex or high-value cases). The TAP panel is specific to the initiative, supported by relevant functional areas, and the actual approval decision is given by the Chief Secretary to the Treasury.

For architects, the practical implication is: if your initiative is likely to need Treasury approval, engage early. The GDS central assurance team will help you prepare, but they cannot rescue a poor business case at the last minute. Architecture decisions that significantly affect cost (platform choices, build-versus-buy decisions, hosting strategy) need to be defensible from a value-for-money perspective because they will face Treasury scrutiny.

A common architect mistake is making architecture decisions that are technically optimal but financially indefensible. Choosing a platform that costs twice as much as the alternative requires a compelling justification in the business case — not just 'it is technically better' but 'it reduces delivery risk by X, reduces time to market by Y, and saves Z in operational costs over five years.' Treasury panels are sophisticated about technology — they will challenge vague claims of technical superiority.

content.heading: Presenting Architecture Decisions in Financial Language
content.body:
The audience for a business case is not architects. It is finance directors, programme boards, investment committees, and potentially Treasury officials. They think in terms of cost, risk, return, and affordability. Your architecture decisions need to be translated into this language.

Cost comparison should be honest and complete. Do not hide costs in one option to make it look cheaper. Include: capital expenditure (build, procurement, migration), operational expenditure (hosting, licensing, support, staffing), and transition costs (dual running, training, decommissioning the old system). Present costs as a clear annual profile showing when money is needed.

Risk quantification should be specific. Do not say 'this option is lower risk.' Say 'this option has a 30% probability of a three-month schedule overrun, which would cost an additional £400,000 in contractor extensions. The alternative has a 10% probability of the same overrun because the technology is more mature and the team has prior experience.' Quantified risk allows decision-makers to factor risk into their value-for-money assessment.

Benefits should be measurable. Do not say 'this architecture is more flexible.' Say 'this architecture reduces the average time to deploy a new feature from 6 weeks to 2 weeks, enabling the department to respond to policy changes 3 times faster. Based on the current rate of policy-driven changes (8 per year), this saves approximately 32 weeks of development time annually, valued at £480,000 at current team cost rates.'

Total Cost of Ownership is the figure that matters. A cloud solution with low capital cost but high annual operational cost may look cheap in year one but expensive over five years. A self-hosted solution with high capital cost but low operational cost may be the reverse. Present the TCO over the business case period (typically 5-10 years for technology) so decision-makers see the full picture.

The Green Book's approach to discounting applies: future costs and benefits are discounted to present values using the Treasury discount rate. This means a benefit delivered in year five is worth less than the same benefit delivered in year one. As an architect, you do not need to do the discounting yourself — the finance team will handle it — but you need to provide the raw cost and benefit profiles accurately.

content.heading: Common Failures in Technology Business Cases
content.body:
Having reviewed hundreds of government technology business cases, certain failure patterns recur. Understanding these helps you avoid them.

The Single Option Business Case presents one option (the one the team wants) and two obviously unviable alternatives. Decision-makers see through this immediately. It signals that the team has already decided and is seeking ratification rather than genuine appraisal. Good business cases present genuinely different approaches — build versus buy, cloud versus on-premise, phased versus big-bang — each with honest advantages and disadvantages.

The Build Cost Only estimate accounts for the cost of building the solution but ignores the cost of running it. In cloud-native architectures, operational costs (compute, storage, data transfer, managed services) often exceed build costs within 18 months. A business case that presents a £2 million build cost without mentioning the £800,000 annual operational cost is misleading.

The Missing Transition plan fails to account for the period of dual running, data migration, user transition, and decommissioning of the system being replaced. Transition costs in government are typically 20-40% of total programme cost because data migration is complex, dual running is expensive, and decommissioning legacy systems takes longer than expected.

The Unrealistic Timeline presents an architecture that cannot physically be delivered in the proposed timeframe. This happens when political pressure sets the deadline before the technical scope is understood. The business case should be honest about what is achievable — offering a phased approach where the most critical capability is delivered first, with subsequent phases completing the vision.

The Benefit Inflation problem occurs when the benefits section claims savings or improvements that are aspirational rather than evidence-based. 'Estimated productivity improvement of 40%' without evidence or methodology will be challenged by any competent investment board. Benefits should be based on evidence from similar initiatives, user research, or measurable current-state baselines.

The Forgotten Dependencies business case presents the initiative in isolation when it actually depends on other initiatives, shared platforms, or organisational changes. If your architecture depends on GOV.UK One Login being available, or on a data sharing agreement being signed, or on another team completing their API, these dependencies must be explicit in the business case because they represent delivery risk.

The Ignored Do-Nothing Option fails to articulate what happens if the investment is not made. In government, the do-nothing option often has significant cost: growing maintenance burden, increasing security risk, inability to meet new policy requirements, or loss of service availability. Quantifying the cost of inaction is often the strongest argument for investment.

content.heading: Aligning Architecture Decisions with Assurance Requirements
content.body:
The Digital Assurance Playbook identifies specific areas that assurance should test. As an architect preparing for internal approval or GDS scrutiny, aligning your architecture with these areas from the start saves significant rework later.

Meeting outcomes: can you clearly state what outcome your architecture enables? Not what it does technically, but what improvement it creates for users, for operations, or for the department. 'This architecture enables 500,000 citizens to check their benefit entitlement online within 30 seconds' is an outcome. 'This architecture uses microservices with event-driven integration' is not.

Avoiding duplication: before your business case proposes building something new, have you checked whether a solution already exists? This means checking GOV.UK shared platforms (Notify, Pay, One Login), checking the Government Assurance Services pipeline for similar initiatives in other departments, and engaging with the GDS Enterprise Architecture team who maintain visibility of cross-government initiatives.

Standards alignment: your architecture should demonstrably align with the Technology Code of Practice, Service Standard, GDS API standards, and Secure by Design principles. Where it deviates, the deviation should be justified and documented. Assurers will check this.

Cloud First: the Government Cloud First policy remains in effect. If your architecture is not cloud-based, you need a compelling justification (data sovereignty requirements, specific hardware needs, or demonstrable cost advantage of on-premise for your specific use case).

Legacy debt: assurers will check whether your initiative tackles existing legacy debt or risks creating new legacy challenges. Using evergreen, always-updated products is highlighted as good practice. Avoid architectures that depend on existing legacy systems or that will themselves become legacy quickly.

ATRS compliance: if your architecture includes algorithmic tools or AI in decision-making processes with public impact, you must publish a record using the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard. This is now mandatory across all government departments and is checked as part of digital assurance.

workedExample.title: Building the Business Case for DESNZ Platform Modernisation
workedExample.context: DESNZ operates 14 digital services on a shared platform built in 2019. The platform uses container orchestration on a managed cloud service, with shared databases and a common API gateway. Over five years, the platform has accumulated significant technical debt: the container orchestration version is approaching end-of-support, the shared databases create deployment coupling between services, and the API gateway cannot support the newer authentication patterns required by GOV.UK One Login integration. The platform team estimates they spend 65% of their capacity on maintenance. The department needs to modernise the platform to support new energy policy services, integrate with GOV.UK One Login, and reduce the maintenance burden. The estimated cost is £8.2 million over three years, which exceeds the £5 million pipeline threshold and approaches the department's DAL.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect leads the technical contribution to the Outline Business Case.

Strategic Case contribution: The architect articulates the problem in terms the investment committee understands. The current platform constrains the department's ability to deliver new services required by legislation (the Energy Act 2023 mandates three new digital reporting services by 2027). Without modernisation, these services cannot be built on the existing platform and would require a separate, duplicative infrastructure at higher long-term cost. The architect quantifies the maintenance burden: £1.8 million per year currently spent on keeping the existing platform running that could be redirected to new capability.

Economic Case contribution: The architect develops four options.

Option 1 (Do Nothing): Continue on current platform. Cost: £9 million over 5 years (growing maintenance). Risk: end-of-support timeline creates security vulnerability. Cannot deliver mandated new services without separate infrastructure.

Option 2 (In-place upgrade): Upgrade the container orchestration, migrate databases to service-owned instances, replace the API gateway. Cost: £8.2 million over 3 years (build) plus £3.5 million over 5 years (operations). Lower risk than full rebuild. Can deliver new services on upgraded platform. Preferred option.

Option 3 (Full rebuild on new platform): Rebuild all 14 services on a new cloud-native platform from scratch. Cost: £14.5 million over 4 years. Lowest long-term operational cost but highest upfront investment and delivery risk. Timeline too long for legislative deadlines.

Option 4 (Managed platform service): Move to a government shared hosting platform. Cost: £6.8 million migration plus £2.1 million annual managed service fee. Reduces operational burden but creates dependency on shared platform roadmap and limits architectural flexibility.

The architect applies 15% optimism bias to the preferred option (appropriate for a programme at OBC stage with well-understood scope), adjusting the build cost to £9.4 million.

Commercial Case contribution: The architect specifies that the modernisation requires specialist Kubernetes engineering (available through the DOS7 framework), cloud architecture consultancy (available through G-Cloud), and potentially a managed database service (available from major cloud providers through existing departmental agreements).

Financial Case contribution: The architect provides the annual cost profile showing how spend is distributed across the three-year build period, demonstrating that the peak year (year 2) requires £3.8 million and is within the department's annual capital allocation for digital.

Management Case contribution: The architect proposes a phased delivery approach — upgrading the container orchestration first (reducing security risk), then decoupling databases service by service (reducing deployment coupling), then replacing the API gateway (enabling GOV.UK One Login integration). Each phase delivers measurable value independently, reducing programme risk.
workedExample.outcome: The investment committee approves Option 2 with a condition that the programme returns at Full Business Case stage with confirmed contractor costs and a detailed phase 1 plan. The initiative is recorded on the Government Assurance Services pipeline. Because it approaches but does not exceed the DAL, it is assured internally by the departmental digital assurance team with GDS providing advisory support on the GOV.UK One Login integration aspects.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The business case succeeded because it connected architecture decisions to outcomes the investment committee cared about: legislative compliance, cost reduction, and risk management. The 'do nothing' option was quantified honestly, showing that inaction was more expensive than investment over five years. The phased approach reduced risk and showed incremental value delivery, which gave the committee confidence that money would not be wasted if the programme encountered problems. The architect's contribution was not just technical — it was translating technical reality into investment language.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Business Case That Got Rejected
civilServiceScenario.background: Your department submitted a £12 million business case to its investment committee for a new case management platform. The case proposed replacing a 15-year-old bespoke system with a modern cloud-native platform. The investment committee rejected the case, citing: 'insufficient evidence of benefits,' 'options not genuinely different,' 'unclear why the cheaper COTS option was rejected,' and 'no evidence that the team has the capability to deliver this.' The programme sponsor is frustrated and has asked you, as the Lead Solution Architect, to help strengthen the resubmission.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You need to diagnose what went wrong with the original business case from an architecture perspective and lead the technical input for a resubmission that addresses the committee's concerns. The timeline is tight — the resubmission is needed within six weeks for the next committee cycle.
constraints: The committee's feedback must be addressed directly — the same case with cosmetic changes will be rejected again
The programme team is convinced their preferred option (custom build) is correct but struggled to articulate why
A COTS vendor has offered a solution at 60% of the custom build cost — the committee wants to understand why this was rejected
The benefits in the original case were qualitative ('improved user experience') rather than quantified
The original case presented three options but two were clearly unviable (do nothing and rebuild on mainframe)
The delivery team is a mix of civil servants and contractors — the committee is concerned about delivery capability
The new system must integrate with 7 other departmental systems, which was not adequately addressed in the original case
The £12 million whole life cost means this must be recorded on the Government Assurance Services pipeline
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Lead Solution Architect responsible for strengthening the technical content of the resubmitted business case. You need to produce genuinely credible options, quantify benefits, and address the COTS question honestly.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
The original case failed because it was advocacy rather than analysis. The architect needs to approach the resubmission with genuine intellectual honesty. This means: seriously evaluating the COTS option (it may actually be viable for some components even if not all), presenting options that are genuinely different (custom build, COTS, hybrid, and phased approaches), quantifying benefits with evidence (measuring current process inefficiencies, timing manual workarounds, counting errors caused by the legacy system), and addressing the capability concern (showing what skills exist, what needs to be recruited, and how the delivery approach manages risk).

The integration challenge is probably the strongest argument against a pure COTS approach — if the platform must integrate with 7 departmental systems, a COTS product may require extensive customisation that erodes its cost advantage. But this needs to be demonstrated with evidence, not asserted.

The architecture lesson is about honesty in business cases. When architects become advocates for their preferred solution rather than analysts of the options, they lose credibility with investment boards. The strongest business cases are the ones where the reviewer can see that all options were genuinely considered and the recommendation is based on evidence rather than preference.

practiceArtefact.description: A programme board has asked you to produce an options appraisal for a new digital service that will allow UK energy suppliers to submit quarterly carbon emissions data to DESNZ. The service will process data from approximately 200 suppliers, validate it against regulatory rules, produce aggregated reports for policy teams, and publish summary data on GOV.UK. Produce a concise options appraisal covering 4 genuine options with cost estimates, risk assessments, and a recommendation.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Present each option with: a one-paragraph description, estimated whole-life cost over 5 years (capital + operational), key advantages, key disadvantages, key risks, and strategic alignment with TCoP. Include a summary comparison table. Make your recommendation explicit and state why the preferred option represents best value for money. Remember to consider: build vs buy, cloud platform choices, reuse of existing departmental components, and integration with GOV.UK shared platforms.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Options Appraisal: Carbon Emissions Quarterly Reporting Service**

Prepared for: Investment Committee | Date: [Date] | Author: [Solution Architect]

**Context:** Mandated by the Energy Act 2023. 200 suppliers must submit quarterly. Service must be live by Q1 2027. Data is OFFICIAL. Must integrate with existing DESNZ data warehouse for analysis.

**Option 1: Custom Build on Existing DESNZ Platform**
Description: Build a bespoke service on the department's existing container platform, using the shared API gateway and deployment pipeline.
5-year cost: £2.8M (£1.6M build, £240K/year operations)
Advantages: Full control, consistent with existing services, team has platform experience, integrates natively with data warehouse.
Disadvantages: Build takes 9 months, ongoing maintenance responsibility, adds another service to platform maintenance burden.
Risks: Platform approaching capacity; this service adds to modernisation scope.
TCoP alignment: Cloud-first, open source stack, integrates with GOV.UK Notify for comms.

**Option 2: GOV.UK Forms + Custom Backend**
Description: Use GOV.UK Forms for the submission interface, build a custom validation and reporting backend.
5-year cost: £1.9M (£900K build, £200K/year operations)
Advantages: Lower build cost, GOV.UK Forms handles accessibility and design patterns, faster to deliver (6 months).
Disadvantages: GOV.UK Forms may not support the complex validation rules needed for emissions data, limited customisation of submission interface.
Risks: Forms capability may not meet requirements — needs spike to confirm feasibility.
TCoP alignment: Strong — reuses shared government platform.

**Option 3: COTS Environmental Reporting Platform**
Description: Procure a commercial environmental reporting platform and configure it for UK carbon emissions requirements.
5-year cost: £3.4M (£400K implementation, £600K/year licensing and support)
Advantages: Fastest to deliver (4 months configuration), vendor handles maintenance and updates, mature product with regulatory reporting features.
Disadvantages: Highest whole-life cost due to licensing, vendor lock-in, limited integration capability with DESNZ data warehouse (requires custom ETL), does not use GOV.UK patterns.
Risks: Vendor dependency, licensing cost escalation at renewal, data residency concerns.
TCoP alignment: Weak — proprietary platform, limited openness.

**Option 4: Extend Existing DEFRA Environmental Reporting Service**
Description: DEFRA operates a similar environmental reporting service. Explore extending it to cover DESNZ carbon emissions requirements.
5-year cost: £1.4M (£800K adaptation and integration, £120K/year contribution to shared running costs)
Advantages: Lowest cost, reuses proven platform, aligns with cross-government reuse principle, shared operational burden.
Disadvantages: Requires DEFRA agreement and prioritisation, may compromise on DESNZ-specific requirements, governance shared between departments.
Risks: Dependency on DEFRA roadmap and capacity, cross-departmental governance complexity.
TCoP alignment: Very strong — exemplifies share and reuse principle.

**Summary Comparison:**
| Criterion | Option 1 | Option 2 | Option 3 | Option 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5-year cost | £2.8M | £1.9M | £3.4M | £1.4M |
| Time to live | 9 months | 6 months | 4 months | 8 months |
| Strategic alignment | Good | Strong | Weak | Very Strong |
| Delivery risk | Low | Medium | Low | Medium |
| Long-term flexibility | High | Medium | Low | Medium |

**Recommendation:** Option 4 (DEFRA extension) if feasibility is confirmed through a 4-week discovery with DEFRA. Fallback: Option 2 (GOV.UK Forms + backend) if DEFRA extension is not viable. Recommend a 4-week feasibility spike before committing, funded from existing programme budget.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a technology investment in your department that was approved. Was the business case genuinely rigorous, or was it advocacy for a predetermined decision? What would you change about the process?
How has the removal of central spend controls affected business case quality in your organisation? Has greater autonomy led to better or worse investment decisions?
When you estimate costs for architecture options, how often are your estimates accurate? What do you consistently underestimate, and what could you do differently?
Have you ever seen a COTS option genuinely evaluated against a custom build? What made the evaluation honest or dishonest?
How would you explain the value of your current architecture programme to a finance director who has no technical background? Can you do it in three sentences?

knowledgeCheck.question: Under the post-RESET framework, when does an initiative require Treasury Approval Process (TAP) panel review?
options: When it exceeds £5 million in whole life cost
When it exceeds the organisation's Delegated Authority Limit or is deemed Novel, Contentious, or Repercussive
When it involves any cloud technology deployment
When it affects more than one government department
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Treasury approval through the TAP is needed when spending exceeds the organisation's Delegated Authority Limit (set by HM Treasury for each organisation) or when HM Treasury deems the initiative Novel, Contentious, or Repercussive. The £5 million threshold is for pipeline reporting, not for Treasury approval.

knowledgeCheck.question: What are the five cases in the HM Treasury Green Book business case model?
options: Technical, Financial, Commercial, Operational, and Risk
Strategic, Economic, Commercial, Financial, and Management
Business, Technical, Security, Delivery, and Benefits
Vision, Options, Costs, Risks, and Plan
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Green Book five-case model consists of: Strategic (why), Economic (which option is best value), Commercial (can it be procured), Financial (is it affordable), and Management (can it be delivered). This is the government's standard framework for all business cases.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the pipeline reporting threshold for digital and technology initiatives under the Digital Assurance Playbook?
options: £100,000 for digital and £1 million for technology
£1 million for all initiatives
£5 million whole life cost for digital and technology, £0 for cryptographic products
£20 million for programmes and £5 million for projects
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Digital Assurance Playbook sets the threshold at £5 million whole life cost for all digital and technology delivery, and £0 for cryptographic products (which must always be reported). Organisations may set their own lower internal thresholds.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common architect failure when contributing to business cases?
options: Providing too many options for the committee to evaluate
Underestimating costs by focusing on build costs and ignoring operational, transition, and whole-life costs
Being too honest about the risks of the preferred option
Providing too much technical detail for the audience
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architects consistently underestimate costs because they focus on build/development costs and forget: integration costs, data migration, testing (security and performance), operational costs (hosting, monitoring, support), training, change management, and decommissioning. Whole-life costing that includes all these elements is essential for credible business cases.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following best describes the architect's role in the business case process?
options: Writing the entire business case and presenting it to the investment committee
Generating credible options, producing realistic cost estimates, identifying technical risks, and defining the delivery approach
Choosing the technology and letting the programme manager build the case around it
Reviewing the business case after the finance team has written it
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architects do not write business cases (that is the programme manager's role) but they are essential contributors. Their primary contributions are: generating genuinely different options, producing realistic whole-life cost estimates, identifying and quantifying technical risks, and defining the technical delivery approach. Without strong architectural input, business cases lack technical credibility.
